title: Solar Quote Comparison Workbook
subtitle: Match the equipment, ownership terms and energy assumptions before ranking the price.
outcome: Complete one matched solar-offer comparison, with unresolved items assigned to the installer, lender or utility. Keep the cash offer, financing agreement, energy model and utility bill scenario distinct.
cover_lines: Cash, financing, lease and PPA records
intro: For U.S. homeowners with two or more actual rooftop-solar proposals. Bring the complete offers, financing disclosures if applicable, recent utility bills and the relevant utility tariff. This is a decision-record workbook, not a system design, credit recommendation or investment forecast.

Read the twelve short modules on pages 3-14. Complete the eight worksheets on pages 15-22. Copy provider questions from page 23. Source limits are on page 24; the final decision review is on page 25. Leave unknowns visible rather than filling them with an optimistic estimate.

Original first edition, October 27, 2026. Personal use includes printing worksheets and sharing your completed records with your own providers and advisers. Do not redistribute or resell the blank book. The purchase is £9.99 GBP; all project examples are invented USD scenarios, not market prices.

Fields do not calculate automatically. Save a copy in a compatible PDF reader, close and reopen it to check persistence. Entries remain in your saved file; this PDF does not upload them. No homeowner trial, purchase demand, savings result or forecast accuracy is claimed.

sections.title: Give each offer a stable identity
paras: Start a separate record for the installation proposal and the payment agreement. The installer, equipment owner, lender and service provider may be different entities. Record their exact names, document dates and revision IDs, then connect the records using one offer ID. A sales slide is not a substitute for the complete documents.

Ask what the offer actually buys: ownership of installed equipment, use of someone else's equipment, or electricity under a power purchase agreement. The FTC's solar consumer guide distinguishes buying, leasing and purchasing power [FTC]. Treat these as different obligations before comparing a monthly number.

Write the household decision in one sentence: for example, compare two ownership proposals for the same assessed roof area without assuming a future tax credit or utility-rate increase. Record roof work, planned occupancy and an expected house sale as questions to resolve, not as reasons to select a payment product automatically.

Your result is a comparison packet, not a recommendation to borrow or sign. Keep the installer scope, lender schedule and utility assumptions separately reviewable. If a salesperson cannot provide a current complete document set, note that limitation and make obtaining it the next action.

sections.title: Match DC capacity and included work
paras: Record panel quantity and each panel's rated watts from the proposal. Quantity multiplied by module watts, divided by 1,000, gives a DC-kW nameplate check. Preserve the provider's stated rating basis; a DC array capacity and an AC inverter rating describe different parts of the system and should not be silently substituted.

List exact model identifiers, inverter or conversion equipment, mounting, monitoring and any storage separately. An advertised 8 kW label does not explain the roof layout, installation boundaries, electrical supporting work, utility process or battery scope. Obtain qualified site-specific answers; do not inspect electrical equipment or create an installation design using this book.

Classify every supporting task as included, excluded, allowance or unresolved. Ask about permit and interconnection work, roof-condition review, service-equipment assessment, access, finish restoration, removal and reinstallation, and ongoing monitoring costs. These are scope questions, not a statement that every home requires the same work.

Use a matched-scope comparison column next to the actual quote. Adding an excluded item for analysis does not amend the contractor's offer. Request a written revision before relying on the adjusted total, and keep uncertainties distinct from confirmed prices.

sections.title: Case 1: the same size, different boundary
paras: Invented USD example: both proposals list 20 modules rated at 400 W each. The nameplate check is 20 x 400 / 1,000 = 8.0 kW DC. Offer A has a cash price of $22,400 but excludes an assessed $1,800 supporting-work package and $600 of application costs. Offer B quotes $24,000 with those same tasks included.

A's headline ratio is $22,400 / 8,000 W = $2.80/W DC. Its matched-scope analysis total is $22,400 + $1,800 + $600 = $24,800, or $3.10/W DC. B's matched price is $24,000, or $3.00/W DC. The analysis difference is $800 in B's favor, assuming all remaining scope is equivalent.

The $2.80/W headline did not prove the better offer. Neither does the matched $3.00/W result prove B has better workmanship or that either price is typical. This exercise tests boundaries and arithmetic only; product differences, warranty support and provider evidence can still change the decision.

Request A's revised all-in cash offer and B's written inclusion confirmation. If either task has an allowance rather than a fixed price, keep the sensitivity visible. Do not add a cost to A twice if its revised price already includes it. Worksheets 1 and 2 preserve the raw and adjusted figures side by side.

sections.title: Separate a production model from a promise
paras: Ask for the production estimate's input record: location basis, roof planes, array orientation, tilt, shading representation, system losses and equipment assumptions. Record annual and monthly kWh with the model name and version or report date. Two quotes can use the same nameplate DC capacity while assuming different energy production.

PVWatts estimates grid-connected photovoltaic production and warns that results depend on inputs and inherent uncertainties [PVWatts]. Its published inputs include DC size, array type, losses, tilt and azimuth. Use provider-prepared reports for a consistent comparison; this workbook has not run a model for your home and supplies no site-specific performance estimate.

A model output, a salesperson's projection and a contractual production guarantee are three different records. For a guarantee, ask for the metric, measurement period, exclusions, remedy and responsible entity in the actual agreement. An annual forecast alone does not establish any compensation obligation.

Request the same input basis from all providers where it is technically appropriate. Where the layouts genuinely differ, retain those differences rather than forcing an artificial equality. Mark unexplained yield differences for clarification. Do not choose a system merely because its forecast uses the largest annual kWh figure.

sections.title: Case 2: equal kWh, unequal value
paras: Invented simplified single-rate scenario: annual generation is 10,000 kWh. The assumed avoided import rate is $0.24/kWh and export compensation is $0.06/kWh. Household A uses 4,000 generated kWh directly and exports 6,000. Its gross modeled energy value is 4,000 x $0.24 + 6,000 x $0.06 = $1,320.

If the same generation instead has 7,000 kWh used directly and 3,000 exported, gross modeled value becomes $1,860. The $540 difference comes entirely from a different use/export split. Crediting all 10,000 kWh at $0.24 would give $2,400 and overstate the first scenario by $1,080 under these assumptions.

Suppose annual household use is 12,000 kWh. In the first scenario, remaining imports are 8,000 kWh costing $1,920, less $360 export credit, plus an assumed $180 fixed charge: a $1,740 modeled utility bill. Without solar the model is $2,880 + $180 = $3,060. Difference: $1,320, consistent with the energy-value method.

This is not a tariff simulation or a promise of savings. It excludes time-of-use rates, demand charges, minimum bills, taxes, credit expiry, financing, maintenance and changes in consumption. Replace assumptions with the utility's actual rules and an appropriate interval model when needed. Do not infer a self-use share from an annual offset percentage.

sections.title: Keep the cash offer beside the loan
paras: Ask for the cash price and the financed price for the identical equipment and installation scope. Record principal, amount financed, down payment, APR, term, required payment sequence, fees and total of payments from the actual disclosures. A difference between prices needs explanation; do not automatically label the entire difference an unlawful fee.

The CFPB's August 7, 2024 solar-financing report describes risks involving embedded markups and payment increases tied to assumed prepayments [CFPB 2024]. It is historical risk context, not evidence of current typical fees or tax eligibility. Use it to frame questions, then verify every term in the offer in front of you.

Make a separate line for any expected lump-sum prepayment. Record its due date, whether it is optional, and what happens to later payments if it is not made. A payment schedule calculated around a presumed benefit does not prove that benefit will arrive or that the household has cash to make the payment.

This workbook does not evaluate credit suitability, recommend a lender or calculate APR. Ask the lender or an independent qualified adviser to resolve disclosure differences. Do not treat the nominal total of payments as a discounted economic comparison, and do not add loan principal again when summing the repayments that already repay it.

sections.title: Case 3: a lower payment is not a lower total
paras: Invented offers for otherwise identical scope: cash price $24,000. Financing A has $29,000 principal and 240 monthly payments of $170, with no down payment or balloon in this demonstration. Financing B has $25,000 principal and 180 payments of $190, again with no down payment or balloon. These are arithmetic inputs, not actual credit offers or stated APRs.

A's nominal scheduled payments total 240 x $170 = $40,800. B's total is 180 x $190 = $34,200. A's monthly payment is $20 lower but its scheduled total is $6,600 higher. Differences from the same $24,000 cash offer are $16,800 and $10,200, respectively; these differences combine the stated pricing and payment assumptions.

Do not add $29,000 to $40,800: those scheduled payments already include repayment of the principal. Do not call the entire $16,800 difference interest, since financed pricing and other terms may differ from cash. Actual lender disclosures are needed to separate fees, finance charges and required totals.

Before ranking, confirm no initial payment period, later reset, financed extra, voluntary prepayment assumption, balloon or separate fee was omitted. Compare the quoted total of payments with your schedule sum and ask for any difference to be reconciled. This case does not establish affordability or recommend financing over cash.

sections.title: Read lease and PPA obligations separately
paras: For a lease, record the payment for use of the equipment and who owns it. For a PPA, record the energy billing basis and price per kWh, including which generated or delivered energy is billable. The FTC distinguishes these structures and emphasizes checking the actual terms [FTC]. Do not assume either structure transfers ownership to you.

Request the year-one payment or energy rate, escalation formula, timing of increases, contract length and every separately charged service. A percentage escalator compounds if applied to the previous year's rate; an increase applied on another basis must be modeled using its actual wording. A fixed starting rate is not necessarily fixed for the term.

For the comparison, keep the solar-provider obligation beside the remaining utility bill. Ask what happens with low production, excess energy, export credits, downtime and any minimum purchase. The same generation forecast can create different payments when one agreement bills all generation and another defines a different quantity.

Assign responsibility for maintenance, roof access, removal/reinstallation, equipment replacement and damage claims. Record the documents and responsible party, not an assumed free service. The workbook is not a lease review or legal interpretation; a qualified adviser should address unclear obligations before commitment.

sections.title: Case 4: escalators and energy billing
paras: Invented lease: $120 per month in year 1, escalating 3% annually on the prior year's payment. Annual year-1 cost = $1,440; year 2 = $1,483.20; year 3 = $1,527.696, rounded to $1,527.70 for display. The three-year sum before rounding is $4,450.896, displayed as $4,450.90. This short horizon does not represent a full contract term.

Invented alternative PPA: 10,000 billable kWh in year 1 at $0.14/kWh = $1,400. Assume a 2% annual rate escalator and the same billable quantity solely for this exercise. Year 2 costs $1,428; year 3 costs $1,456.56. The three-year total is $4,284.56, a $166.34 difference from the displayed lease total.

The lower three-year PPA total is not proof of a better long-term option. Quantities, actual escalation wording, maintenance, purchase options, utility charges and termination obligations may differ. If PPA billable quantity in year 2 is 11,000 instead, the $0.1428 rate produces $1,570.80, rather than $1,428.

Show each year and billing basis, keep full precision for intermediate math, and reconcile the contract's actual rounding rule. Do not extrapolate a flat annual generation input into a performance prediction. Get the complete provider schedule before comparing the whole term or estimating the cost of an early sale.

sections.title: Verify a benefit before subtracting it
paras: Keep gross installation cost, contractual payments and any potential incentive in separate rows. Record program name, primary source, eligible recipient, qualifying date, conditions, application step and expected timing. Mark a claim unverified until its relevant terms are checked. Do not use an unverified benefit as a down payment source.

As checked October 27, 2026, the IRS Residential Clean Energy Credit page says the credit is unavailable for property placed in service after December 31, 2025 [IRS]. This workbook therefore assumes no new homeowner federal credit in its examples. Do not import the 30% credit discussion from the 2024 CFPB report into a new 2026 installation scenario.

A provider's statement about a business incentive is not evidence that the homeowner receives that amount. Ask who is eligible, who owns the equipment and whether any benefit is already reflected in the quoted price. Do not subtract it again. This book does not assess commercial-credit qualification, state incentives or individual tax circumstances.

For any separately verified local benefit, keep a no-benefit scenario alongside the conditional one. Confirm deadlines and eligibility with the administering authority and, where appropriate, a qualified tax adviser. Do not combine a promised rebate, a utility export credit and a production forecast into one guaranteed savings number.

sections.title: Plan for the roof, service and a future sale
paras: Create an event register rather than a prediction of trouble. Ask who you contact for production concerns, monitoring outages, roof work, equipment faults and warranty claims. Record labor, shipping and access exclusions as questions when they are not clear. A product warranty and a provider's service promise can have different responsible parties.

If roof repair becomes necessary, request the removal and reinstallation terms and how workmanship or weatherproofing responsibilities are handled. Obtain qualified roof and electrical assessment as needed; this workbook does not judge whether the roof or service is suitable. Keep any supporting-work quote outside the solar scope until explicitly included.

For a possible home sale, ask about notice, transfer approval, buyer qualification, loan payoff, buyout, early termination and end-of-term removal or purchase options. The FTC highlights contract terms and sale-related considerations [FTC]. Do not assume a buyer will accept the agreement or that a transfer will be free.

Record which answers must come from the installer, lender, equipment owner, utility or adviser. Ask for the exact clause or price schedule and retain its version. A verbal assurance that everything is transferable should not close the question without the relevant documentation.

sections.title: Make a decision record without a false score
paras: First screen for unresolved essentials: incomplete scope, unexplained price differences, missing payment terms, unsupported production inputs or unclear transfer obligations. A weighted score cannot turn a missing obligation into a harmless small deduction. Assign each blocker an owner and the evidence needed to resolve it.

Then compare actual offers and matched assumptions side by side. Keep the original provider number, your analysis adjustment and the resulting comparison number in separate places. Where a material difference cannot be normalized honestly, explain it in words rather than inventing a price for it.

Write a short conclusion: which offer remains under consideration, which assumptions drive that conclusion and what could change it. The appropriate outcome may be another written clarification or independent assessment. Record the final document set before any commitment; the worksheets themselves do not authorize installation or financing.

Existing HomeCostEngine energy and contractor books cover general bills, scope and budgeting. This title adds solar-specific ownership, DC/AC and production records, use/export valuation, loan payment checks and lease/PPA schedules. Its prose, four cases and worksheet prompts are new. Buy it only if that focused comparison packet is useful to your decision.

questions: Which entity owns the equipment, supplies service and receives payments?
Can you provide a cash price for exactly the same scope as the financed offer?
What is the DC array rating, inverter AC rating and exact equipment list?
Which roof, electrical, permit and utility tasks are included or unresolved?
Can you provide production inputs and monthly kWh, with model/report date?
Which production promise is contractual, and what remedy and exclusions apply?
What utility tariff and self-use/export split support the bill illustration?
What payment reset, lump sum, fee or balloon appears in the full schedule?
For a lease or PPA, what escalates and which energy quantity is billable?
Who receives any incentive, under what current source and qualifying date?
Who handles maintenance, roof work, transfer and end-of-term removal?
Which revised documents resolve the remaining essential gaps before commitment?
sources: Buying, leasing and PPA distinctions; bid and contract-review context. Used for limited general consumer facts, not current tax eligibility.
August 7, 2024 historical report: embedded financing costs and assumed-prepayment risks. Its tax-credit and market data are not current 2026 guidance.
National Laboratory of the Rockies model: input-dependent energy estimates and explicit uncertainty. No home-specific model run or endorsement is claimed.
Current page explicitly excludes property placed in service after December 31, 2025. Used narrowly for that cutoff; individual tax advice is outside scope.
source_limits: Primary links checked October 27, 2026. Official pages can include older passages: the IRS placed-in-service cutoff is used rather than older phaseout wording elsewhere on the page. The 2024 CFPB report is used only for financing-risk context. Local utility tariffs and program eligibility must be checked for the actual home. Our scenarios, worksheets and decision sequence are independently authored; no source endorses the workbook.
overlap: General energy-bill, contractor-scope and budget concepts overlap with existing HomeCostEngine books. No substantive passage or case is reused. The new output is a solar-specific offer packet linking equipment, ownership, modeled energy value, payment obligations and transfer evidence. The free companion article gives a checklist and one cash-scope example; the book adds the complete eight-sheet workflow and three additional cases.
final_checks: Can someone else locate the exact installation, financing and ownership documents behind your comparison? Archive superseded revisions.
Have you kept DC kW, AC kW, kWh and USD distinct, with the provider's model inputs and the utility's billing assumptions?
Are cash price, financed obligation, lease payment or PPA energy rate compared on the same stated scope and horizon? Keep unresolved differences visible.
Have unverified benefits been excluded from the base case, with any historical source clearly dated? Confirm current program terms independently.
Are service, roof-work, sale-transfer and end-of-term responsibilities supported by the actual agreement? Get appropriate professional review for uncertain obligations.
Does your decision identify the remaining question, its responsible provider and the evidence needed? A request for clarification is a valid outcome.

Save and reopen your completed PDF. Use the free companion checklist at https://homecostengine.com/blog/why-same-size-solar-quotes-differ . No forecast here establishes demand for this book or the performance of a solar installation.
